name: Carpet Weaving
description: Iranian carpet weaving encompasses distinct regional approaches to materials, knots, patterns, and loom construction. Kashan and Fars illustrate the variety of the craft, while surviving historical carpets reveal connections between textile design and other arts.

seo.title: Iranian Carpet Weaving: Kashan, Fars and Historical Design
seo.description: Explore regional carpet traditions in Iran, from Kashan's asymmetrical knots to the portable looms of Fars and the designs of Safavid silk carpets.

content.heading: Reading a carpet through its construction
content.content:
A carpet can be understood through its structure as well as its pattern. The Metropolitan Museum of Art's Silk Kashan Carpet, dated to the sixteenth century, has silk in its warp, weft, and pile. Warp threads form the lengthwise foundation; weft threads cross that foundation; pile supplies the raised surface. The museum identifies this example as asymmetrically knotted. These details describe how an object was made, rather than simply what its decoration resembles. [s1]

Its title also introduces an important caution. The museum attributes the carpet to Iran, probably Kashan, and explicitly acknowledges uncertainty about the origins of many historical Persian carpets. A familiar place-name can therefore express a scholarly attribution rather than a documented workshop address. For readers encountering carpets in museums, retaining words such as 'probably' is part of understanding the evidence. [s1]

content.heading: Kashan: knots, colour and an established design vocabulary
content.content:
Kashan, a city in central Iran, is associated with carpets using the asymmetrical knot, also called the Persian knot. Visit Iran describes a repertoire that includes central medallions, vase and tree compositions, hunting scenes, and the curved boteh motif familiar internationally as paisley. Its account also identifies crimson fields with dark blue borders among characteristic colour arrangements. These are useful points of recognition, rather than a checklist that every Kashan carpet must satisfy. [s2]

Dyeing is a related specialist activity. The same account names pomegranate skins, walnut skins, and grape leaves among materials used for traditional colours. Identifying these ingredients explains the relationship between weaving and dye preparation, but does not establish the dye composition of an individual carpet. Visit Iran records the inscription of Kashan's traditional carpet-weaving skills on UNESCO's Representative List in 2010. [s2]

content.heading: Fars: portable looms and different knotting traditions
content.content:
Fars, in southern Iran, offers another setting for carpet production. Visit Iran's account emphasizes weaving among pastoral communities, including the Qashqai, and describes horizontal looms whose portability suited movement with livestock. It records both symmetrical and asymmetrical knots, with choices differing between communities and designs. The labels 'Turkish knot' and 'Persian knot' consequently should not be read as a simple division between the carpets of two countries. [s3]

The described motifs include plants, stars, birds, and other animals. Lion imagery appears in Qashqai gabbeh, a regional carpet form. This range matters because a regional tradition contains internal differences: technique, composition, and community cannot be reduced to a single recurring emblem. Visit Iran records the UNESCO inscription of Fars carpet-weaving skills in 2010. [s3]

content.heading: Designs that travelled between media
content.content: The Met's silk example places weaving within the wider arts of the Safavid period. Its medallions have counterparts in bookbinding and manuscript illumination, while cloud bands and peonies reflect motifs originating in Chinese art and incorporated into Safavid design. The museum suggests that pattern books may have helped transmit such imagery. Looking at construction, attribution, and shared ornament together reveals a craft shaped by both local expertise and wider artistic exchange. [s1]

name: Basket Weaving
description: Iranian basketry includes containers, mats, trays, and screens made through several ways of combining plant fibres. Kapu from Khuzestan provides a particularly well-documented example of material knowledge, household learning, and adaptation to new markets.

seo.title: Basket Weaving in Iran: Regional Fibres and Khuzestan Kapu
seo.description: Discover Iranian basketry through regional plant materials, kapu construction, household apprenticeship, and the experiences of a Khuzestan weaver.

content.heading: A family of practical objects
content.content: Basketry in Iran extends beyond baskets. Encyclopaedia Iranica's account of twentieth-century crafts includes mats, tent screens, trays, fans, and lidded containers made by interlacing, twining, or coiling fibres. It associates reed baskets with southern lowlands around Behbahan, Bushehr, and Bandar Abbas, and records relief-patterned rush mats in Mazandaran on the Caspian coast. Qashqai storage boxes combine reeds with coloured wool. This historical survey shows why the category is best approached through materials, construction, and use rather than one national basket shape. [s1]

content.heading: Kapu: building around a plant-fibre core
content.content:
Kapu is associated particularly with Dezful and nearby villages in Khuzestan, southwestern Iran. Visit Iran describes a flexible plant material called kertak forming a core around which palm leaflets are worked. Young, pale leaflets are soaked before use. Coloured wool can cover parts of the surface or create a more extensively covered exterior. Material and colour are therefore connected to construction, rather than being decoration applied to a finished rigid vessel. [s2]

The account distinguishes versions using palm leaflets, versions covered with yarn, and combinations of the two. It also describes an expanded range of sizes and objects, including fruit bowls, coasters, and vases, responding to market demand. These variations show how a recognizable craft can accommodate new uses. The same source warns that the core is sensitive to humidity, an important qualification to general claims about the durability of plant materials. [s2]

content.heading: Learning through company and correction
content.content:
An interview published by the retailer Zan Artefacts offers a maker's perspective. The weaver, identified by the protective pseudonym Armaya, recalls watching her mother, aunt, and other relatives before practising alongside friends. Her account of an older woman correcting a difficult basket lid makes apprenticeship concrete: seeing a finished object was only part of learning how to resolve a construction problem. [s3]

She describes weaving as both pleasurable work and a source of money she can spend independently. Her stated household uses include storing sewing equipment, jewellery, and other small possessions; she also makes coordinated baskets for brides. These details connect basketry to domestic organization and personal decisions. They are one person's testimony, published by a business selling the work, and cannot establish typical earnings or working conditions across Khuzestan. [s3]

content.heading: From household container to international design object
content.content:
The Victoria and Albert Museum's shop provides a specific example of kapu reaching an overseas retail setting. Its listing credits Zan Artefacts and identifies date-palm leaves, kertak, and wool as the materials of a small Iranian basket. The record supports the existence of that product and sales channel; it does not measure the size of the export trade or the maker's share of the retail price. [s4]

Read alongside Armaya's account, this example suggests a useful way to understand continuity: follow the relationship between an object's construction, the maker's choices, and its intended use. Basketry can remain rooted in learned skills while entering a different setting and acquiring a new audience. That interpretation does not require assuming that every basket follows an unchanged ancient pattern. [s3][s4]

name: Traditional Pottery
description: Traditional pottery in Iran encompasses varied methods of shaping, decorating, and firing clay. Kalpurgan's unglazed vessels offer a focused example, while archaeological evidence provides a much longer history that must be distinguished from claims of uninterrupted modern continuity.

seo.title: Traditional Pottery in Iran: Clay, Kalpurgan and Historical Evidence
seo.description: Understand Iranian pottery through archaeological context, regional forming and firing methods, and the unglazed vessels made by women in Kalpurgan.

content.heading: Everyday vessels as historical evidence
content.content:
Pottery helps archaeologists investigate ordinary life because vessels were widely used and ceramic fragments survive well. The Milwaukee Public Museum explains that their analysis can illuminate activities, economies, beliefs, and social organization. Its overview places some early Iranian pottery in the Neolithic period, around the seventh millennium BCE. This is a broad archaeological timescale, not a founding date for a present-day craft community. [s1]

Before the potter's wheel, vessels could be built by coiling clay or forming it around a mould. The museum describes similarities between early pottery from the Iranian plateau and neighbouring regions to the west, including Mesopotamia and Anatolia. It also discusses the appearance of painted geometric, animal, and symbolic decoration. These comparisons place pottery within regional exchange and experimentation rather than treating it as an isolated national invention. [s1]

content.heading: Several ways to shape and fire clay
content.content:
Encyclopaedia Iranica's historical survey records different forming and firing arrangements within Iran. Near Kalpurgan it describes women shaping vessels on a simple rotating support made from nested saucers with sand between them. Its account of Asalem in the Talesh region of northern Iran describes similar supports but different clay preparation and firing enclosures. These observations document local technical choices; they should not be turned into a ranking of communities as more or less advanced. [s2]

The survey also reports competition from plastics, metal vessels, and inexpensive imported ceramics. Because its evidence concerns twentieth-century crafts, this is historical context rather than a measurement of market conditions in 2026. [s2]

content.heading: Kalpurgan: an unglazed regional tradition
content.content:
Kalpurgan is a village in Sistan and Baluchestan, southeastern Iran, near the Pakistan border. Visit Iran describes pottery made mainly by women without a potter's wheel. The vessels are unglazed, with clay that becomes red after firing and geometric or abstract painted decoration. Bowls, jars, jugs, and drinking vessels are among the forms it identifies. [s3]

The account describes drying the shaped vessels before applying a mineral pigment prepared from a stone called tituk. The stone is ground, mixed with water, and applied using a thin palm twig. Firing darkens the painted designs. Men are described as supplying the clay, while women undertake the principal forming and decorative work. This division of tasks shows that the finished vessel depends on linked activities, including obtaining and preparing materials. [s3]

content.title: The documented Kalpurgan production sequence
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Obtain local clay"] -->|"Prepare material for shaping"| B["Form vessels by hand"]
  B -->|"Dry before decoration"| C["Dry shaped vessels"]
  C -->|"Apply mineral pigment with a palm twig"| D["Paint geometric designs"]
  D -->|"Harden vessels and darken decoration"| E["Fire vessels"]
```
content.summary: The arrows show the sequence described by Visit Iran. This is a regional account, not a universal recipe for Iranian pottery.

content.heading: Recognizing continuity without overstating it
content.content: Visit Iran compares Kalpurgan pottery with archaeological finds and presents its methods as an ancient inheritance. Resemblance, however, does not by itself demonstrate an unbroken sequence of identical practice. The defensible distinction is between the long archaeological history of pottery in Iran and the specifically documented techniques of a living community. Keeping both in view allows the vessels to be understood as skilled work with historical depth, without assigning their makers an unsupported claim of technological immutability. [s1][s3]
